profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting is being held between the inpatient nursing unit and the hospital's clinical informatics team two weeks before a pilot launch of an electronic health record (EHR)-prepopulated nurse handoff report on the 32-bed cardiac step-down unit, 5 South. The context is a quality-improvement initiative based on recent internal findings that standardized, prepopulated handoff reports may reduce omissions, shorten nurse-to-nurse handoff time, and improve patient experience scores related to nurse communication. The agenda is to confirm the report version being launched, clarify who is included in the pilot, review what the teams mean by a 'complete' handoff for evaluation purposes, and coordinate the support/feedback handoff between bedside nursing and informatics during go-live week. The expected outcome is an apparently smooth agreement on launch readiness, pilot coverage, and feedback flow, even though several underlying assumptions remain misaligned.

members.name: Danielle Ruiz
members.role: Nurse Manager, 5 South Cardiac Step-Down Unit
members.expertise: Inpatient nursing operations, shift handoff workflow, staffing coordination, patient experience improvement
members.background: Danielle is a former charge nurse who has managed 5 South for four years and has led bedside handoff standardization efforts, including adapting the unit's SBAR worksheet to reflect common cardiac step-down needs.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to feel immediately helpful to bedside nurses, reduce complaints about rushed shift change, and avoid burdening her already stretched staff with extra troubleshooting or duplicate documentation.
hidden_assumptions: The 'current handoff template' means the March unit worksheet version her nurses have been using informally, including prompts for wounds, behavior, and family concerns.
A 'complete' handoff means a receiving nurse can give or receive report without needing to open additional chart tabs for the practical details that usually cause callbacks later.
If the tool is being rolled out 'on 5 South,' that naturally includes float nurses and travelers assigned there because the handoff happens on the unit, not by employment category.
Feedback to informatics should be filtered through charge nurses or super-users and consolidated, because bedside nurses should not have to interrupt workflow to file individual tickets.

members.name: Evan Park
members.role: Clinical Informatics Analyst, Inpatient EHR Optimization Team
members.expertise: EHR build governance, clinical workflow mapping, report configuration, go-live support, quality reporting
members.background: Evan supports inpatient nursing documentation projects across the hospital and translated the approved handoff requirements into the Epic report build after the proposal was reviewed by the documentation governance committee.
members.private_state: He wants a controlled pilot that stays within approved build scope, produces clean evaluation data, and minimizes informal change requests that cannot be traced back to governance or support logs.
hidden_assumptions: The 'current handoff template' means the last governance-approved specification attached to the February change request, not later unit-side worksheet edits that were never submitted as build revisions.
A 'complete' handoff for pilot evaluation means all mapped discrete data elements populate reliably for required sections, even if nurses still add contextual details from elsewhere.
A rollout 'on 5 South' refers to the named pilot user group attached to the unit's training and security list, not every temporary clinician who happens to work a shift there.
Post-go-live issues should be submitted as individual EHR support tickets tagged to the pilot so the team can trace errors by user, patient context, and timestamp.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'current handoff template' is being prepopulated
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about launching the prepopulated version of 'the current handoff template.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the March unit worksheet version that nurses have been using in practice, which includes added prompts for wounds, behavior, and family concerns.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the February governance-approved handoff layout in the build ticket, which does not include those later unit-added prompts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe there is only one legitimate 'current' handoff form because the title and general structure are the same, so the phrase sounds perfectly unambiguous in a coordination meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss improving 'information completeness' and say the new report should make handoff more complete.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a receiving nurse can manage report smoothly without hunting through other chart locations for the details that commonly matter during bedside care, even if some nuance is still entered manually.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the required mapped clinical fields auto-populate accurately and consistently in the report, regardless of whether nurses still consult separate tabs for behavioral or family-context details.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Information completeness sounds like a shared, evidence-based objective from the project itself, so each person assumes the other is using the same standard without needing to define it.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included in 'the 5 South rollout'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the pilot is being rolled out 'on 5 South' and refer to 'all 5 South handoffs.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes any nurse handing off patients on 5 South during the pilot, including float pool staff and travelers assigned there.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes only permanent or specifically rostered 5 South staff who are part of the pilot training group and security configuration.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds geographic rather than personnel-based, so it creates a natural illusion of agreement unless someone explicitly distinguishes location from user-group membership.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that staff should 'send issues to informatics' and that week-one feedback will be 'captured.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects charge nurses to gather comments during shifts and bring a consolidated list to the scheduled debrief, except for urgent patient-safety problems.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects bedside nurses or super-users to submit individual help desk tickets tagged to the pilot as issues happen so analysts can investigate specific cases.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are aligned on destination and intent, so the meeting language centers on ownership of the feedback loop rather than the submission mechanism, which each assumes is obvious.

turns.inner_thought: I want to make sure next Monday is still real and that this won't create extra work at shift change. If we're launching the prepopulated version of the worksheet my nurses have actually been using on the unit, it could finally make report feel more useful instead of one more project layered on top of staffing strain.
turns.utterance: I just wanted to confirm we're still on for next Monday with the prepopulated handoff report on 5 South. From the nursing side, I want to make sure our workflow and coverage plans are lined up before we get into the final stretch.

turns.inner_thought: The build is essentially done; we're validating against the February governance-approved handoff specification, which to me is the current handoff template. I mainly need confidence that the unit is ready to use what was approved, not reopen scope through informal local edits.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's still the target. We're in final validation now against the current handoff template, so from my end it's mostly about making sure the unit feels ready from a workflow standpoint.

turns.inner_thought: Good. The nurses have settled into the March worksheet version, especially those extra prompts around wounds, behavior, and family concerns. If that current handoff template is what they'll see opening in the chart, adoption should be much easier and we can avoid the usual pushback about missing practical details.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. Staff have responded pretty well to the latest version of the template, and a lot of them have said the added prompts have made report more usable. If that current report is what's opening in the chart, I think they'll adapt quickly.

turns.inner_thought: She's confirming comfort with the approved layout, which is great. The important thing for evaluation is that the mapped discrete fields populate consistently: diagnosis, code status, lines, fall risk, diet, labs. If those required sections are reliable, we can legitimately say information completeness improved even if nurses still reference other parts of the chart.
turns.utterance: Great. On the build side, diagnosis, code status, lines, fall risk, diet, and recent labs are all mapping cleanly now, so I would expect information completeness and handoff speed to improve pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: That all matters, but the real test is whether the receiving nurse can get through report without clicking around for the things that trigger callbacks later, especially confused patients or complicated family situations. If the report still forces them into extra tabs, bedside staff won't experience that as complete no matter how clean the mapped fields are.
turns.utterance: That sounds good, and I agree the goal is better information completeness. As long as nurses can give a complete report without bouncing around the chart too much, especially in the more involved cases, I think they'll feel the benefit right away.

turns.inner_thought: Time to pin down the pilot list. For me, 'on 5 South' means the trained pilot users tied to the unit roster and security setup. I need the final names so reminders, access, and evaluation stay controlled and we don't muddy the data with untrained users.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On rollout logistics, the 5 South pilot reminders will go out to the trained user group as soon as I get the final roster, so I want to make sure we have that buttoned up this week.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send the staffing list we have for the unit. Since the rollout is on 5 South, that should naturally include floats and travelers who are taking assignments there; otherwise shift handoff will be inconsistent from one nurse to the next. They need the same report as everyone else if we're going to avoid confusion at change of shift.
turns.utterance: Absolutely, I can send over the staffing list. We have a few different people covering 5 South this month, and I think they'll appreciate using the same handoff report as everyone else on the unit once we go live.

turns.inner_thought: For week one I need traceable support data, not hallway comments. If issues go straight to informatics as tagged tickets, we can see who experienced what, in which patient chart, and when. That keeps pilot evaluation clean and any fixes within normal support governance.
turns.utterance: Perfect. And for go-live support, any issues that come up in week one should go straight to informatics so we can tune the report quickly. We definitely want that feedback captured while it's fresh.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. I'll have the charge nurses collect comments as people use it and bring a consolidated list to Friday's debrief, unless there's a true urgent problem that needs escalation sooner. I do not want bedside nurses stopping in the middle of report to file separate requests unless something is clearly unsafe.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll have my charge nurses keep an ear on it across shifts and send issues to informatics so week-one feedback is captured. Then we can come into the Friday debrief with a clean list, unless something urgent comes up before then.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that sounds like we'll have enough input to analyze. Once the first week is done, I'll compare handoff duration and information completeness against baseline using the pilot users' data and the mapped field performance. That should be enough for the quality team update if we keep the scope controlled.
turns.utterance: Sounds like a plan. Once the week-one feedback is in, I'll look at handoff duration and information completeness against baseline and put together the pilot update for the quality team.
